analysis.one_liner: Sends every adult $1,000 a month during the pandemic, recouped from top earners.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended, with only 4 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have sent recurring emergency payments to everyone in the United States during the COVID-19 crisis: $1,000 a month for each adult ($2,000 per married couple) and $500 per child, continuing until the pandemic was officially declared over. The payments would be advanceable and delivered monthly rather than waiting on tax season, with an expedited sign-up process for people not in the tax system. The money would not count as income for taxes and would not count against eligibility for other benefits. Only the highest earners, above roughly $250,000 for singles and $500,000 for couples, would have to repay the full rebate at tax time.
analysis.who_benefits: Every adult resident and every dependent child would receive monthly cash payments for as long as the pandemic emergency lasted, including people with little or no tax liability and people not required to file returns. The payments would not reduce anyone's eligibility for unemployment insurance, SNAP, Medicaid, or other aid.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable credit of $1,000 per adult ($2,000 per joint return) plus $500 per qualifying child, payable in advance on a monthly basis for as long as the COVID-19 emergency continues [S2][S3].

Payments would go out monthly 'as rapidly as possible,' with a pro rata first payment, and would continue until the pandemic is formally declared over by the Treasury and Health and Human Services secretaries, with Congress able to extend them afterward [S3].

The Treasury Secretary must set up an expedited application process so people can get payments using 2018 or 2019 tax data or alternative submissions, rather than waiting for the annual tax return [S2][S3].
The rebates would not count as income for federal, state, or local taxes, and would not count as a resource when determining eligibility for any federal or federally funded benefit program [S3].
Only high earners would repay: a 100 percent clawback applies to the rebate amount above thresholds of $250,000 in adjusted gross income for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers [S3].

Payments would also reach residents of U.S. territories including Puerto Rico, and the bill appropriates about $360 million to Treasury, IRS, and Social Security Administration to run the program [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, on an open-ended basis until the pandemic is certified over. Households earning above $250,000 (single) or $500,000 (joint) would repay their rebates in full, so the net cost would fall mainly on deficit spending shared by all taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; top earners repay rebates

drawbacks.text: The program is open-ended and tied to a certification by the Treasury and HHS secretaries that the pandemic is over, giving two executive officials control over when a universal payment program ends [S3].

Payments go to nearly everyone, including households well above the clawback thresholds, so a large share of the money would go out and then be clawed back later, adding administrative cost and complexity; the CRS summary notes the credit is denied only to certain top income earners [S2][S3].
The bill was never scored by the Congressional Budget Office, so its total cost was never formally estimated, and it would have been deficit-financed [S1][S5].

Broad universal checks are a blunter tool than expanding unemployment insurance or targeted aid, a tradeoff the bill itself acknowledges by saying the payments 'should supplement' those programs rather than replace them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households facing lost income in the pandemic, recurring monthly cash is more protective than a one-time check, and the design is unusually generous to low-income people: payments are advanceable, non-taxable, and exempt from benefit eligibility calculations. The honest costs are fiscal (an open-ended universal program with no CBO score) and administrative (clawing back payments from high earners after the fact). The design tradeoff between universality and targeting is real but debatable in both directions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on March 19, 2020, in the first weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no further action of any kind [S5].
Only 4 members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats [S4].
The bill never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No concentrated interest had to fight this bill; it simply never moved. The recurring-payment idea died quietly in committee while Congress pursued other relief vehicles, and the bill's open-ended spending never happened. Low-income households are the clearest losers, since recurring monthly payments of this kind were never enacted in any form.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one had to act; the idea died in committee

for.name: Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 19, 2020 and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every named supporter was a Democrat (the sponsor plus 4 Democratic cosponsors), no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would have required these households to repay 100 percent of their rebate at tax time, so the cost of universal payments would land partly on them. The clawback was never enacted.

The bill appropriated roughly $360 million in administrative funds and would have created an open-ended universal payment obligation until the pandemic was certified over. The cost would have been deficit-financed.
